summary.text: A solvable group is a group that can be constructed from abelian groups using extensions.
Equivalently, taking commutator subgroups over and over eventually reaches the trivial subgroup, and the number of steps needed is the derived length.
Solvability matters for equations: Sₙ is not solvable for n > 4, a key step in showing some high-degree polynomials cannot be solved by radicals.

facts.label: Feit–Thompson theorem
facts.value: Every finite group of odd order is solvable

facts.label: Groups below order 60
facts.value: All are solvable, since the smallest simple non-abelian group is A₅

items.prompt: A student says abelian groups are too simple to count as solvable. Who is right?

options.label: The student, because solvable groups must be non-abelian
Abelian groups are solvable, trivially, as the basic example
Only finite abelian groups qualify as solvable
Only abelian groups with a prime number of elements qualify

items.explain: Abelian groups are the basic example: the group itself followed by the trivial group already forms the required series.

items.prompt: G is a solvable group and H sits inside it as a subgroup. What can you say about H?

options.label: H may or may not be solvable
H must be abelian
H must be non-solvable
H is solvable too

items.explain: Every subgroup of a solvable group is solvable.

items.prompt: A group G has a normal subgroup N. Both N and the leftover quotient group are solvable. What follows for G?

options.label: G is solvable too
G is abelian
Nothing can be said about G
G is simple

items.explain: G is solvable if and only if both N and G/N are solvable.

items.prompt: A finite group has an odd number of elements. What does the Feit–Thompson theorem tell you about it?

options.label: It must be abelian
It must be simple
It is solvable
It might fail to be solvable, depending on its size

items.explain: The Feit–Thompson theorem states that every finite group of odd order is solvable.

items.prompt: Why does the group of all rearrangements of five or more items matter for polynomial equations?

options.label: It is abelian, so every equation is solvable
It is not solvable, a key step in showing some equations resist radicals
It is nilpotent, so quintics reduce to quartics
It is the smallest group order below sixty

items.explain: Sₙ is not solvable for n > 4, a key step in the proof that for every degree above four some polynomials are not solvable by radicals.

items.prompt: You take a group, then its commutator subgroup, then that group's commutator subgroup, and so on. What outcome shows the original group is solvable?

options.label: The sequence never changes after the first step
The sequence grows into a larger group
The sequence alternates between two groups
The sequence eventually reaches the trivial subgroup

items.explain: A group is solvable exactly when its derived series, built from repeated commutator subgroups, reaches the trivial subgroup at a finite stage.
